svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM): how it finds the 3D shape of molecules."], [1, "A purified sample is spread in a thin film on a grid."], [3, "The grid is plunged into liquid ethane: the water freezes as glass-like ice."], [5.5, "A transmission electron microscope images thousands of molecules in many orientations."], [8, "A computer sorts and averages particle images by orientation."], [10.5, "The views are combined into a 3D map."], [13, "An atomic model is built into the map."]]
svg.title: Cryogenic electron microscopy
svg.desc: The cryo-EM workflow: purified sample on a grid, plunge-freezing in vitreous ice, imaging many particles in a transmission electron microscope, 2D classification and averaging, 3D reconstruction and an atomic model.
svg.text: Cryo-EM: from frozen sample to 3D structure

g.data-info: Many copies of the same molecule (e.g. a protein complex) in a thin film of water on a small grid.
The grid is plunged into liquid ethane so fast that water freezes as glass-like (vitreous) ice, not crystals, keeping molecules in their natural shape.
At about −180 °C, with a low electron dose to limit damage. Each image shows thousands of molecules in random orientations.
A computer sorts hundreds of thousands of particle images by orientation and averages each group to improve the signal.
The averaged views are combined into a three-dimensional map of electron density.
A model of the protein chain is built into the map, at up to near-atomic resolution. Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2017.

g.text: • molecules frozen in their natural, hydrated shape
• works for large complexes and membrane proteins
• used to solve the SARS-CoV-2 spike in weeks (2020)
